title: FAQ
text:
Why is PHES-EF needed?

Public health environmental surveillance, such as wastewater-based surveillance, expanded rapidly during the COVID-19 pandemic, but there is still no agreed way to evaluate how well these systems work. PHES-EF will provide a shared framework for doing so. Read more on the About page.



What is a Delphi consensus study?

The Delphi method is an iterative, multi-round survey approach that uses controlled feedback to build consensus among a group of people while keeping their responses anonymous (1,2). PHES-EF will use an online (e-Delphi) survey with two rounds, followed by a consensus meeting. See the Delphi study page for details.



When will the study take place?

Registration for e-Delphi panellists will open in January 2027. Round 1 will run in March 2027, Round 2 will run from April to May 2027, and the consensus meeting will be held in September or October 2027. See the study timeline for details.



Who is eligible to participate in the study?

The eligibility criteria for e-Delphi survey panellists can be found on the Delphi study page.



What will I be asked to do?

In Round 1, you will rate whether each candidate item in your expertise pathway should be included in the framework, using a 7-point scale, and you can suggest new items. In Round 2, you will rate new items and re-rate items that did not reach consensus on four properties. You can try an example question on the Work to date page.



How long will the survey take?

Each round will take about an hour to complete and will stay open for about five weeks, so you can complete it when it suits you. There will be two rounds. See the Delphi study page for details.



How will my data be used and protected?

Only anonymous responses will be used for analysis. All data will be password protected, and only approved members of the study working group at the Ottawa Hospital will have access. Anonymous aggregate data will be shared on our Open Science Framework (OSF) project page when the study is complete. See the declarations on the About page for details on ethics approval and privacy.



Where can I find study documents?

The study protocol, scoping review protocols, executive group Terms of Reference, presentations and recruitment materials are on the Documents page and our OSF project page.

text:
PHES-EF is in its second step: generating the candidate evaluation items that panellists will rate in the e-Delphi survey. Two scoping reviews have mapped how surveillance systems are evaluated across public health, animal health, One Health and wastewater-based surveillance. The identified terms have been reconciled into a draft framework, which the executive group will review before the survey opens in 2027. This page summarizes that work and gives a glimpse into what panellists will see when completing the survey.

  3ReconcileTerms matched across disciplines, recording synonyms and related terms.
  4OrganizeTerms arranged into themes, domains and attributes, then reviewed by the executive group.



Evaluation terms are not used the same way in every field. The same word can mean different things, and the same idea can go by different names. Each term in the framework records its synonyms (“also known as”) and related terms (“see also”), so readers from any discipline can find it.

Acceptability and engagement brings together terms that different disciplines call acceptability, engagement or participation. Here is everything a candidate item records, with a short definition of each field.


Delphi candidate item
Acceptability and engagement
Attribute A measurable property or characteristic.


Where it sits in the framework


Theme
Partnerships and community engagement
A high-level grouping of related concepts that define broad areas of public health evaluation.


Domain
Community engagement; Professional partnerships
A major area of focus within a theme. An item can sit in more than one domain.


Subdomain
None (not needed here)
A specific aspect or perspective within a domain.




What it means

Definition A concise definition derived from the scoping review literature that captures the essential meaning of the concept.
The willingness of individuals and organizations to participate in the surveillance system and the depth of their active involvement. (CDC 2001; Calba 2015; Goutard 2022; Hoinville 2013)


Synonyms Terms used in other disciplines or sources for the same concept.
Acceptability; engagement; participation


See also Related terms that provide additional context or relevance to the main schema term.
Collaboration; governance; simplicity



Evidence from the scoping reviews

DescriptionAn explanation of the term that builds on the definition.

Acceptability and engagement capture the willingness of actors and end-users to contribute to a surveillance system and the degree to which they are actively involved in its processes. (Hoinville 2013; Calba 2015) The two constructs are conceptually linked: willingness (acceptability) is a prerequisite for active involvement (engagement), while sustained engagement reinforces acceptability over time. Reporting burden is the primary constraint on willingness: a system that is difficult or time-consuming to contribute to will see participation rates fall regardless of its public health value, while actors who receive timely feedback are more likely to remain actively involved. (CDC 2001; Goutard 2022) Trust in the system and among actors, and the degree to which the system respects cultural context and privacy, shape both constructs across settings. (Azofeifa 2018; Auer 2011; Calba 2015) Because acceptability is constrained by reporting burden, it co-varies with simplicity, and engagement is more easily sustained when actors receive feedback through communication and dissemination channels that demonstrate the value of their participation. (Goutard 2022; Drewe 2015)



BackgroundThe historical development, theoretical foundations and evidence base that establish the concept’s importance in surveillance system evaluation.

Acceptability was formally defined in the surveillance evaluation literature in 1988 as “the willingness of individuals and organizations to participate in the surveillance system”. (CDC 1988) The updated guidelines kept this definition while expanding the influencing factors to include community participation, data feedback to reporting sources, and confidentiality protections. (CDC 2001) The combined construct of acceptability and engagement first appeared in standardized terminology for animal health surveillance, defined as “the willingness of persons and organisations to participate in the surveillance system, and the degree to which each of these users is involved in the surveillance process”. (Hoinville 2013) This expanded definition was then put into practice through participatory diagramming methods (relational, flow and impact diagrams) to assess actor roles, information flows and trust within surveillance systems (Calba 2015), and later formalized in the AccePT toolkit, which assesses objective adequacy, operational satisfaction, role recognition and trust among actors. (Goutard 2022)
Public health frameworks have treated acceptability primarily as a willingness construct. (CDC 1988; CDC 2001; Groseclose 2010; Azofeifa 2018) In animal health, the SERVAL framework relabelled the concept “participation”, the extent to which user groups “get involved in the surveillance process”, explicitly incorporating the engagement dimension. (Drewe 2015) One Health and multi-sectoral evaluations expanded it to include institutional trust and political will across contributing sectors, highlighting mutual understanding and willingness to collaborate. (Bordier 2020; Innes 2022) In wastewater-based surveillance, evaluators assessed “the extent to which end-users and stakeholders were willing to participate in the pilot WS and in the future”. (Amato 2023) In Indigenous community surveillance, acceptability was linked to cultural appropriateness and to community ownership and control of data. (Auer 2011) Acceptability and engagement is now widely recognized as a combined, multi-dimensional attribute that encompasses willingness, active involvement and trust.



Evaluation methods (9)The methods or tools used to quantify an attribute.


Participation rate analysis: the proportion of potential reporting sources actively contributing, including agency participation rates, physician and laboratory reporting rates, and interview completion rates (CDC 1988; CDC 2001; Groseclose 2010).
Report form completeness review: the proportion of required data fields completed per submitted report (CDC 1988; Albali 2023).
Questionnaire or survey of actors and end-users: structured or semi-structured instruments assessing willingness to continue participating, perceived value, and factors influencing participation (Amato 2023; Albali 2023).
Likert-scale ratings: five-point scales assessing agreement with statements about system performance or willingness to participate (Albali 2023).
Key-informant interviews: qualitative interviews with actors and end-users to explore perceptions of acceptability and barriers to engagement (Harper 2011; Auer 2011).
Participatory diagramming tools (AccePT/RISKUR): relational diagrams, flow diagrams with proportional piling, and impact diagrams to assess actor relationships, satisfaction with information flow, and trust (Calba 2015; Calba 2016; Goutard 2022).
Focus groups: structured discussions with surveillance actors to surface systemic factors affecting willingness and involvement (Calba 2015).
OASIS flash evaluation: criterion-based assessment across 20 indicators grouped into categories such as organization, animation, resources, feedback, training and partnerships (Calba 2015).
Process evaluation: review of procedures, completion times, training adequacy and dissemination processes through field observation and record review (Auer 2011).

title: Study design
text:
PHES-EF is being developed using an established, internationally recognized consensus methodology. The study follows its published protocol and will be reported using the ACCORD guideline for consensus studies, with PRISMA-ScR for the scoping reviews and GRIPP2 for public involvement. This approach ensures:


Evidence-based content through two systematic scoping reviews
International consensus via a two-round e-Delphi survey and a consensus meeting
Diverse perspectives from content experts, knowledge users and engaged members of the public
Transparent development with open sharing of materials and progress on the Open Science Framework
Broad applicability across public health environmental surveillance systems, using wastewater-based surveillance as an example


The framework will be developed in five steps.





1





Agree on the scope of the study and develop the study protocol
Agree on terms of reference for executive group members

Completed



2





Conduct scoping reviews to extract candidate items for the e-Delphi survey (searches are being updated)
Review candidate items with the executive group for organization, completeness and redundancy

In progress



3





Recruit, screen and register international panellists (registration will open in January 2027)
Run two online survey rounds in spring 2027

Upcoming



4





Hold a hybrid or virtual consensus meeting in September or October 2027
Reach expert consensus on the final list of items and agree on dissemination strategies

Upcoming



5





Post a preprint to OSF, then submit to an open-access peer-reviewed journal (late 2027), under a CC BY-SA 4.0 licence
Engage researchers and knowledge users, and support adoption of the framework

Upcoming




A multinational and multidisciplinary executive group oversees the development of the evaluation framework. The group brings expertise from various fields, including public health, infectious disease and epidemiology; environmental and physical sciences; mathematical sciences; social sciences; communication, knowledge translation and exchange; knowledge users; and an engaged public.
The executive group is responsible for providing feedback on the framework development process (e.g., framework organization, completeness, additions, redundancy), supporting and advising working groups in their area of expertise, connecting the study to other related projects, recruiting e-Delphi panellists, participating in the consensus meeting, disseminating the evaluation framework, advising and/or participating in post-publication activities, and promoting the adoption of the evaluation framework among their professional networks. Co-chairs are also responsible for decision-making when the executive group cannot reach a consensus, leading executive group activities, and the overall framework development process.
For more information about the members of the study’s executive group, please visit the Team page.



We are systematically compiling a list of e-Delphi candidate items through two scoping reviews, content analysis and extraction, and executive group consultation. The scoping review searches are being updated. See Work to date for progress so far.
You can view relevant scoping review registrations and publications on our Documents page.



PHES-EF will use an e-Delphi survey, an online version of the Delphi method, in which panellists rate candidate items over two anonymous rounds with feedback between them (1,2). Running the survey online allows panellists to take part from anywhere, across time zones.
Key dates are in the timeline below. For details on recruitment, eligibility, rating and consensus, see the Delphi study page.



In preparation for the consensus meeting, the study working group will categorize the remaining candidate items for consideration into a preliminary evaluation framework. This will include merging and/or modifying the remaining items based on gathered feedback from the e-Delphi rounds.
A hybrid or virtual consensus meeting will be held in September or October 2027, using the Surveylet Delphi survey platform, after the results of the e-Delphi have been compiled and analysed. The primary objective of the meeting will be to achieve expert consensus on the final list of items for PHES-EF, through review and discussion of salient items. This process will be guided by the empirical evidence that was identified during the scoping reviews, and the opinions gathered during the e-Delphi process. The secondary objective will be to discuss publication and dissemination strategies for the final evaluation framework.
Steps to produce the final list of items are as follows: (i) present the results of the e-Delphi exercise (name, rationale, and score of each item); (ii) discuss the rationale and relevance for including the items in the framework; and (iii) vote on equivocal and non-consensual items. PHES-EF will be developed based on the final list of items that receive consensus during the executive group consensus meeting.



The development of the evaluation framework will be reported in a statement document that will include the rationale and a brief description of the meeting, and the panellists involved. While the publication strategy will be finalized based on the consensus meeting discussion, the preliminary approach will be to post to OSF, as a preprint, before submission to an open-access peer-reviewed journal in late 2027. During this time, we will actively seek feedback from experts, knowledge users, and the public within our networks and via social media. PHES-EF will be made available under an open licence (CC BY-SA 4.0).

Panellists will complete a short screening questionnaire. Recruitment will continue during both rounds.

Panellists will rate each candidate item for inclusion and suggest new items. Round 1 will be open for about five weeks and take about an hour.

title: About
text:
PHES-EF (Public Health Environmental Surveillance Evaluation Framework) is an international consensus study to develop a framework for evaluating public health environmental surveillance systems, using wastewater-based surveillance as an example.


Public health environmental surveillance, which monitors health threats using samples from the environment, expanded rapidly during the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic. Wastewater-based surveillance is the most prominent example. As these systems diversify and become part of routine public health practice, there is still no agreed way to evaluate them, and standard methods for analysing and reporting their data remain unclear (1).
A shared evaluation framework will help public health agencies, decision-makers and researchers to:


Judge whether a surveillance system is effective and provides a return on investment
Strengthen accountability, transparency and public trust
Plan for sustainability
Compare system performance across settings using consistent methods






Evaluation framework definition: An evaluation framework is a structured system designed to systematically assess the effectiveness and impact of a program (2,3). It typically outlines key components (such as domains, concepts, and indicators or measures) that should be included in an evaluation. It also provides a logical organization of these components, explains the process by which they were identified and prioritized, and may offer guidance on how to measure them. By offering a comprehensive and transparent basis for evaluation, such frameworks support informed decision-making and help identify areas for improvement in public health programs.

PHES-EF organizes these components into four levels, from broad to specific:




Theme
A high-level grouping of related concepts that define broad areas of public health evaluation.
Example: Surveillance effectiveness


Domain
A major area of focus within a theme.
Example: Ascertainment performance


Subdomain
A specific aspect or perspective within a domain.
None needed for this example


Attribute
A measurable property or characteristic.
Example: Sensitivity





PHES-EF is being developed through an international e-Delphi consensus study. Candidate items come from two scoping reviews of how surveillance systems are evaluated. A panel of content experts, knowledge users and engaged members of the public will rate these items over two anonymous online survey rounds, followed by a consensus meeting. See Study design for the five study steps and timeline, and the Delphi study page for how the survey works.

“Equity is defined as the removal of systemic barriers and biases enabling all individuals to have equal opportunity to access and benefit from the program” (4). To achieve this, members of the research team are committed to developing a strong understanding of the systemic barriers faced by individuals from underrepresented groups.
“Diversity is defined as differences in race, colour, place of origin, religion, immigrant and newcomer status, ethnic origin, ability, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and age” (4). Panellists will be asked to provide characteristic information (e.g., country of residence, gender, primary discipline) to assess and help ensure (through more targeted recruitment) a large diversity in perspectives.
“Inclusion is defined as the practice of ensuring that all individuals are valued and respected for their contributions and are equally supported” (4). To help ensure that all research team members are integrated and supported, we will have a code of conduct statement in the executive group Terms of Reference.
All study working group members will complete EDI-related Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR) Training, and the First Nations principles of Ownership, Control, Access and Possession (OCAP©) training for the research (5). The executive group will receive an overview of EDI and OCAP and will be encouraged and supported to complete such training. Furthermore, staff trained in EDI and OCAP principles will review the framework from an EDI perspective to ensure appropriate language.





To ensure accurate and transparent reporting of knowledge users and public involvement throughout the study, we will refer to the Guidance for Reporting Involvement of Patients and the Public (GRIPP2) checklist (6). We will document the methods used to engage knowledge users, report the impacts and outcomes of their engagement, and report on lessons learned from the experience.

title: Delphi study
text:
A Delphi technique will be used to develop an internationally accepted evaluation framework for public health environmental surveillance. The Delphi method is an iterative multi-round approach that uses a series of sequential surveys, interspersed by controlled feedback, to elicit consensus among a group of individuals while maintaining anonymity (1–4). An electronic Delphi (e-Delphi) method will be used to overcome geographic barriers and allow us to engage panellists internationally across various time zones.
The study protocol is published in PLOS ONE. The preprint is also available on medRxiv.

Key dates for the survey and the rest of the study are in the timeline on the Study design page.


We will recruit a multinational, multidisciplinary panel of wastewater-based surveillance experts, knowledge users, and engaged members of the public to complete the e-Delphi survey. Panellists will be selected to capture the multiple perspectives of those that influence the design, implementation, evaluation, use, and reporting of wastewater-based surveillance activities, including the following discipline subgroups: public health, infectious disease and epidemiology; environmental and physical sciences; mathematical sciences; social sciences; and communication, knowledge translation and exchange.
We will aim to recruit at least 50 panellists, preferably with at least 8 to 10 people per discipline subgroup. Registration will open about four weeks before Round 1, and recruitment will continue during both rounds. Panellists will complete a short screening questionnaire and then receive an anonymous link to the survey. The study working group will monitor the distribution of registered panellists based on their demographic information and will try to distribute appropriately across discipline subgroups and other demographic markers.






Content experts

Definitions: Professional experience: paid employment or professional practice in a listed specialization (current or former). Graduate or professional degree: Master or PhD in a listed discipline/specialization.





We will conduct a two-round e-Delphi survey to generate consensus on evaluation criteria (see the figure below). Summaries of Round 1 will be compiled for the subsequent round. Custom expertise pathways will be generated for each panellist group and discipline subgroup, so panellists will be shown the candidate items most relevant to their expertise. Within each expertise pathway, panellists will also have the option to skip items or self-declare that they are not qualified to assess certain candidate items.


Panellists will rate each candidate item shown to them in their expertise pathway on whether it should be included in an evaluation framework, using a 7-point Likert scale. Candidate items will be generated from scoping review results and consultation with the study executive group. Free-text boxes will be included for panellists to provide feedback or suggest new candidate items for the next round. Items that reach consensus in Round 1 will not be re-rated in Round 2.
Round 1 will be open for about five weeks, take about an hour to complete, and include two email reminders.



Regardless of whether they participated in the previous round, panellists will be invited to participate in Round 2 of the e-Delphi survey. All panellists will be invited to rate new items and re-rate previous items that did not reach consensus. Items in Round 2 will be rated across four rating properties (see below). When re-rating their level of agreement, panellists will be presented with their previous round scores alongside the aggregate group results. Anonymous feedback from Round 1 will also be compiled and presented during Round 2. Any newly suggested items during Round 2 will be deliberated on during the consensus meeting.



In Round 2, candidate items will be assessed on the following four rating properties: (1) relevance and practical utility; (2) scientific rigour, validity and reliability; (3) feasibility, adaptability and resource implications; and (4) equity, inclusiveness, and mitigation of bias.
A 7-point Likert scale (1 = highly irrelevant to 7 = highly relevant) will be used to rate each property. A summary score for each candidate item will be created by calculating the median of the four property ratings. In Round 1, the single inclusion rating is used directly. Panellist ratings will then be categorised as excluded item (irrelevant: 1–2), further discussion (equivocal: 3–5), or core item (relevant: 6–7). Consensus for each item is defined as ≥ 70% of the panellist votes falling within the same category (1–2, 3–5, or 6–7).




e-Delphi consensus process
Round 1: initial candidate items are rated in an anonymized e-Delphi survey. With consensus, items are excluded (irrelevant), sent for further discussion at the consensus meeting (equivocal) or kept as core items (relevant); items without consensus go to Round 2. Round 2: new and non-consensus items are rated the same way; equivocal and non-consensus items go to the consensus meeting. Consensus meeting, hybrid or online with discussion and a Delphi survey: with consensus, items are excluded, optional (equivocal relevance) or core; items without consensus are excluded.

text:
We will recruit a multinational, multidisciplinary panel of wastewater-based surveillance experts, knowledge users, and engaged members of the public to complete the e-Delphi survey. Panellists will be selected to capture the multiple perspectives of those that influence the design, implementation, evaluation, use, and reporting of wastewater-based surveillance activities, including the following discipline subgroups: public health, infectious disease and epidemiology; environmental and physical sciences; mathematical sciences; social sciences; and communication, knowledge translation and exchange.

title: Delphi study
text:
We will conduct a two-round e-Delphi survey to generate consensus on evaluation criteria (see the figure below). Summaries of Round 1 will be compiled for the subsequent round. Custom expertise pathways will be generated for each panellist group and discipline subgroup, so panellists will be shown the candidate items most relevant to their expertise. Within each expertise pathway, panellists will also have the option to skip items or self-declare that they are not qualified to assess certain candidate items.


Panellists will rate each candidate item shown to them in their expertise pathway on whether it should be included in an evaluation framework, using a 7-point Likert scale. Candidate items will be generated from scoping review results and consultation with the study executive group. Free-text boxes will be included for panellists to provide feedback or suggest new candidate items for the next round. Items that reach consensus in Round 1 will not be re-rated in Round 2.
Round 1 will be open for about five weeks, take about an hour to complete, and include two email reminders.



Regardless of whether they participated in the previous round, panellists will be invited to participate in Round 2 of the e-Delphi survey. All panellists will be invited to rate new items and re-rate previous items that did not reach consensus. Items in Round 2 will be rated across four rating properties (see below). When re-rating their level of agreement, panellists will be presented with their previous round scores alongside the aggregate group results. Anonymous feedback from Round 1 will also be compiled and presented during Round 2. Any newly suggested items during Round 2 will be deliberated on during the consensus meeting.



In Round 2, candidate items will be assessed on the following four rating properties: (1) relevance and practical utility; (2) scientific rigour, validity and reliability; (3) feasibility, adaptability and resource implications; and (4) equity, inclusiveness, and mitigation of bias.
A 7-point Likert scale (1 = highly irrelevant to 7 = highly relevant) will be used to rate each property. A summary score for each candidate item will be created by calculating the median of the four property ratings. In Round 1, the single inclusion rating is used directly. Panellist ratings will then be categorised as excluded item (irrelevant: 1–2), further discussion (equivocal: 3–5), or core item (relevant: 6–7). Consensus for each item is defined as ≥ 70% of the panellist votes falling within the same category (1–2, 3–5, or 6–7).




e-Delphi consensus process
Round 1: initial candidate items are rated in an anonymized e-Delphi survey. With consensus, items are excluded (irrelevant), sent for further discussion at the consensus meeting (equivocal) or kept as core items (relevant); items without consensus go to Round 2. Round 2: new and non-consensus items are rated the same way; equivocal and non-consensus items go to the consensus meeting. Consensus meeting, hybrid or online with discussion and a Delphi survey: with consensus, items are excluded, optional (equivocal relevance) or core; items without consensus are excluded.
